Summary:

Bennion et al. investigate how semantic relatedness proactively benefits the learning of new word pairs. The authors draw predictions from Osgood (1949), which posits that the degree of proactive interference (PI) and proactive facilitation (PF) of previously learned items on to-be-learned items depends on the semantic relationships between the old and new information. In the current study, participants subjects learn a set of word pairs ("supplemental pairs"), followed by a second set of pairs ("base pairs"), in which the cue, target or both words are changed, or the pair was identical. Pairs were drawn from either a narrower or wider stimulus set and were tested after either a 5 minute or 48 hour delay. The results show that semantic relatedness overwhelmingly produces PF and greater memory interdependence between base and supplemental pairs, except in the case of unrelated pairs in a wider stimulus set after a short delay, which produced PI. In their final analyses, the authors compare their current results to previous work from their group studying the analogous retroactive effects of semantic relatedness on memory. These comparisons show generally similar, if slightly weaker, patterns of results. The authors interpret their results in the framework of recursive reminders (Hintzman, 2011), which posits that the semantic relationships between new and old word pairs promotes reminders of the old information during the learning of the new to-be-learned information. These reminders help to integrate the old and new information and result in additional retrieval practice opportunities that in turn improve later recall.

Strengths:

Overall, I thought that the analyses were thorough and well-thought-out and the results were incredibly well-situated in the literature, especially with the additional clarification and framing that the authors have made in response to reviewer comments. In particular, I found that the large sample size, inclusion of a wide range of semantic relatedness across the two stimulus sets, variable delays and the ability to directly compare the current results to their prior results on the retroactive effects of semantic relatedness were particular strengths of the authors' approach and make this an impressive contribution to the existing literature. I thought that their interpretations and conclusions were mostly reasonable and included appropriate caveats (where applicable).

Weaknesses:

The changes and additional analyses that the authors have made have addressed my concerns about their analyses. Including the additional Fig 1- Supp 1, panel C greatly helps with the interpretability across stimulus sets, and the additional analyses the authors have performed teasing apart whether cue and target similarity separately influence memorability and interdependence seem to support the rest of their conclusions.

claims.claim: The effects in the ΔTarget condition arise from competing processes of impairments between competing responses at retrieval that have not been integrated versus retrieval benefits when integration has occurred.

claims.claim: The ΔCue condition largely resulted in more consistent proactive facilitation than the ΔTarget condition.

claims.claim: In the ΔBoth condition, changes to both cues and targets mean that both relatedness values need to be relatively high for remindings to occur.

claims.claim: Semantic relatedness, by increasing the likelihood of remindings, provides a mechanism by which existing memories can become more accessible and associated with new learning as part of integrated memory representations.
claims.source: We propose that semantic relatedness, by increasing the likelihood of remindings, provides a mechanism by which existing memories can become more accessible and associated with new learning as part of integrated memory representations that preserve targets and their contexts.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the overall results.

claims.claim: Osgood did not predict proactive interference in the ΔCue condition.
claims.source: However, he did not predict PI in the ΔCue condition, and additionally, we found weak support for PF inching towards the cue and target identity point along the 2-D part of the surface in the ΔBoth condition (which was present in the retroactive narrower stimulus set, 48 hr experiment of our prior paper).

claims.claim: Retroactive benefits are greater than proactive benefits, presumably because target responses receive retrieval practice during remindings.
claims.source: By showing stronger retroactive than proactive benefits here, we propose that the retroactive benefits are greater, presumably because target responses receive retrieval practice during remindings.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the between-experiment comparisons.

claims.claim: Original associations tend to face interference after new, conflicting learning, but slowly recover over time and often eventually eclipse memory for the new information (spontaneous recovery).
claims.source: Additionally, these effects partially resemble those on spontaneous recovery, whereby original associations tend to face interference after new, conflicting learning, but slowly recover over time (either absolutely or relative to the new learning) and often eventually eclipse memory for the new information (Barnes and Underwood, 1959; Postman et al., 1969; Wheeler, 1995).

results.result: High semantic relatedness between initial and later-learned information produces proactive facilitation at longer delays in the narrower stimulus set. In the narrower stimulus set with 48 hr delay, all experimental conditions (ΔCue, ΔTarget, ΔBoth) showed significantly better memory than the Control condition, with No Δ > ΔCue > ΔTarget > ΔBoth > Control pattern. This demonstrates that high semantic relatedness profoundly benefits later-learned memories and produces proactive facilitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 provide converging statistical evidence from the narrower stimulus set experiments showing proactive facilitation effects. The 48 hr delay experiment shows clear ordering across conditions with significant differences (F(4,796)=116.3, p<0.001), and all experimental conditions exceeded the Control condition. The 5 min delay showed similar but weaker patterns. The statistical tests are appropriate and sample sizes adequate (N=200 per experiment).

results.result: Lower average semantic relatedness produces proactive interference in the ΔTarget condition at short retention intervals. In the wider stimulus set with 5 min delay, the ΔTarget condition showed significant proactive interference relative to Control (No Δ > ΔCue = Control = ΔBoth > ΔTarget pattern, F(4,796)=8.50, p<0.001). This interference effect was eliminated at the 48 hr delay.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 and C81 provide statistical evidence for proactive interference under specific conditions (wider stimulus set, short delay, ΔTarget condition). The ANOVA and follow-up t-tests are appropriately conducted with adequate sample size. The finding that PI occurs only with lower relatedness and short delays is well-documented with proper statistical comparisons.

results.result: In the wider stimulus set with 48 hr delay, target relatedness produces a crossover effect where low relatedness causes proactive interference and high relatedness causes proactive facilitation within the ΔTarget condition. Semantic relatedness significantly predicted memorability (r²=0.36, p<0.001), with the lowest third showing PI (t(14)=-3.6, p=0.003) and upper third showing PF (t(14)=4.4, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 and C82 provide strong statistical evidence for the crossover effect. The correlation analysis shows a significant relationship between relatedness and memorability, and the tertile split analysis confirms both PI and PF at different relatedness levels. The regression analysis showing a significantly negative y-intercept further supports the PI at low relatedness. Statistical methods are appropriate.

results.result: Semantic relatedness increases memory interdependence between initial and later-learned pairs across multiple conditions and delays. Interdependence significantly increased with target relatedness in 48 hr experiments (r²>0.11, p<0.02) and was marginally significant in 5 min experiments. Cue relatedness increased interdependence in all experiments (r²>0.08, p<0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C58, C62, and C64 provide consistent evidence across multiple conditions that relatedness increases interdependence. The correlation analyses are appropriately conducted with adequate sample sizes. The pattern is more robust at longer delays, which is theoretically consistent. The interdependence measure is operationalized clearly as frequency of both-correct or both-incorrect responses.

results.result: Intrusions decreased with target relatedness in the wider stimulus set, 48 hr experiment (r²=0.43, p<0.001), supporting the remindings account that relatedness allows building interdependent yet contextually discriminable representations rather than merged representations that cause source confusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 provide evidence against a simple interference account and support the remindings framework. The strong negative correlation between relatedness and intrusions contradicts predictions that relatedness would increase source confusion. This finding, combined with the interdependence results, supports the theoretical interpretation. The statistical analysis is appropriate.

results.result: Cue relatedness increased memorability in both 48 hr experiments (r²>0.09, p<0.02) but not in 5 min experiments. In the wider stimulus set, 48 hr experiment, there was PI at low cue relatedness (lowest third: t(14)=3.0, p=0.009) and PF at high cue relatedness (upper third: t(14)=3.5, p=0.003).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C63 provide statistical evidence for cue relatedness effects on memorability. The correlation analyses and tertile split analyses are appropriately conducted. The pattern parallels the target relatedness findings, showing delay-dependent effects and a crossover from PI to PF with increasing relatedness in the wider stimulus set.

results.result: In the ΔBoth condition, cue+target relatedness did not affect memorability in any experiment (r²<0.03, p>0.48) but improved interdependence in all experiments except the wider stimulus set, 5 min delay experiment (r²>0.07, p<0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 report null findings for memorability but positive findings for interdependence in the ΔBoth condition. The statistical analyses are appropriate, and the null results are properly reported with effect sizes and p-values. The dissociation between memorability and interdependence effects is interesting but the authors acknowledge this differs from their prior retroactive study.

results.result: Semantic relatedness accelerates learning of paired associates. Higher cue and target relatedness produced faster base pair learning (fewer trials to criterion) in most experiments. In the narrower stimulus set, the pattern was No Δ < ΔCue < ΔTarget < ΔBoth < Control (all p<0.008), and cue relatedness (r²>0.064) and target relatedness (r²>0.04) correlated with faster learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C65-C72 provide consistent evidence that relatedness accelerates learning. The trials-to-criterion measure is appropriate, and the statistical analyses (ANOVAs, correlations) are properly conducted with adequate sample sizes. The pattern of results is consistent across experiments, with most correlations reaching significance or marginal significance. This supports the scaffolding interpretation.

results.result: Retroactive benefits are greater than proactive benefits for semantically related information. In the narrower stimulus set, 48 hr experiments, memory was better in the retroactive experiment for ΔCue, ΔTarget, and ΔBoth conditions (all p<0.011) but not Control (p=0.43). Similar patterns were found in the wider stimulus set for ΔCue and ΔTarget conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C85, and C94 compare across experiments without random assignment, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation (C85). While the comparisons use the same stimuli, procedures, and populations, and show consistent patterns across multiple conditions, the lack of random assignment and potential temporal confounds (experiments run at different times) limit the strength of this conclusion. The authors appropriately caveat these findings.

results.result: Testing order does not account for retroactive versus proactive differences. A flipped test experiment (testing supplemental pairs first after retroactive learning) showed no significant differences from the original retroactive experiment (all adjusted p>0.87) but still showed better memory than the proactive experiment in ΔCue, ΔTarget, and ΔBoth conditions (all p<0.002).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide evidence from a control experiment (N=200) designed to rule out testing order as an explanation for retroactive-proactive differences. The statistical comparisons are appropriate and show that the flipped test experiment replicates the retroactive advantage, suggesting testing order is not the primary factor. This strengthens the interpretation of the retroactive-proactive comparisons.

results.result: Combining narrower and wider stimulus sets using the common GloVe metric confirms the main findings. At 48 hr delay, memorability correlated with relatedness in ΔCue (r²>0.29, p<0.001) and ΔTarget (r²=0.2, p<0.001) conditions, and interdependence increased with relatedness in all three conditions (r²>0.16, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 demonstrate that the main findings hold when using a common metric across stimulus sets. This addresses potential concerns about comparing different relatedness metrics (AS vs. GloVe). The combined analyses have larger sample sizes (N=90 pairs) and show consistent patterns, strengthening the overall conclusions. Statistical methods are appropriate.

results.result: The experimental design used five experiments (N=1000 total) with systematic manipulation of semantic relatedness, learning order, and retention interval. Subjects learned 36 supplemental pairs followed by 45 base pairs to criterion, with counterbalancing across five conditions and testing after 5 min or 48 hr delays. Two stimulus sets varied relatedness ranges using AS (0.03-0.96) or GloVe metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C98-C110 describe the experimental design and methods. The design is well-controlled with appropriate counterbalancing (C102), adequate sample sizes (N=200 per experiment), and systematic manipulation of key variables. The use of two relatedness metrics and two delays allows comprehensive testing of the theoretical predictions. Exclusion criteria are clearly stated (C109). The twin-companion design to the prior retroactive study (C7) is appropriate.

results.result: The results generally support Osgood's 1949 predictions about how relatedness affects memory, showing that PI shifts to PF along the ΔTarget line and that PI generally does not occur along the ΔCue line. However, the results diverge from Osgood's predictions in finding some PI in the ΔCue condition and weak support for PF in the ΔBoth condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C30-C33, C43, and C93 relate the current findings to Osgood's theoretical framework. The results provide substantial support for the general predictions while identifying specific deviations (C93). The comparison to the prior retroactive study (C6, C43) strengthens the conclusions. The theoretical framework provides useful organization for the complex pattern of results.

results.result: The authors propose that semantic relatedness increases the likelihood of remindings during new learning, which provides a mechanism for proactive facilitation by creating integrated yet contextually discriminable memory representations. This remindings-based account explains how relatedness can produce both interference (when integration fails) and facilitation (when integration succeeds).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C86-C92 present theoretical interpretations and mechanistic proposals. While the data are consistent with the remindings framework (especially the intrusion data in C54-C55 and interdependence findings), the authors acknowledge they did not directly measure remindings during learning (noted in Discussion limitations). The competing processes explanation (C89) is speculative. The theoretical proposals are plausible but require additional direct evidence.

results.result: The tendency to study memory with short delays and without interrelationships among study material led to the predominance of interference ideas in 20th century memory research.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 makes a broad historical inference about the field of memory research based on the current findings. While the data show that interference effects are limited to specific conditions (short delays, low relatedness), the claim about the historical development of the field is speculative and not directly tested. This is more of a discussion point than a supported empirical result.

results.result: High semantic relatedness between initial and later-learned information produces profound proactive facilitation at longer delays, while low relatedness can produce proactive interference. This represents the core finding that semantic relatedness profoundly benefits later-learned memories, with the direction of effect depending on the level of relatedness.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this central finding. The editor states the study 'provides compelling evidence that semantic relatedness proactively benefits memory' and 'demonstrates the boundaries of these proactive benefits, showing that when studied items have weaker semantic relationships, proactive interference may be observed.' Reviewer 1 describes this as 'one of the central results' showing 'a stronger semantic relationship between a base pair and an earlier pair has a facilitative effect.' Reviewer 2 notes the study 'compellingly shows that relatedness typically leads to proactive facilitation' with interference 'being thus an exception rather than a rule.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'semantic relatedness overwhelmingly produces PF' except 'in the case of unrelated pairs in a wider stimulus set after a short delay, which produced PI.'

results.result: Semantic relatedness increases interdependence between initial and later-learned pairs, with this effect being significant in 48-hour delay experiments and present across multiple experimental conditions. Interdependence increases with both cue and target relatedness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently accept the interdependence findings. Reviewer 2 states 'the study informs our understanding of memory integration, demonstrating how interdependence of memory for related information increases with relatedness.' Reviewer 3 notes the results show 'semantic relatedness overwhelmingly produces...greater memory interdependence between base and supplemental pairs.' The interdependence analyses are described as having 'more converging' results across stimulus sets and metrics compared to memorability analyses.

results.result: Semantic relatedness accelerates learning of paired associates, with higher cue and target relatedness producing faster base pair learning across experiments. Previously learned supplemental pairs scaffold and hasten learning of base pairs depending on their level of relatedness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the learning acceleration findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions 'analyses of learning data, demonstrating that relatedness leads to both better final memory and also faster initial learning' as an 'additional strength' of the study. Reviewer 1 notes the finding that 'semantic relationship prompts retrieval of the earlier pair' which facilitates learning. No reviewer questions these learning speed results.

results.result: In the narrower stimulus set with high overall relatedness, proactive facilitation was observed at 48-hour delay across ΔCue, ΔTarget, and ΔBoth conditions. In the wider stimulus set with lower average relatedness, proactive interference was found in the ΔTarget condition at 5-minute delay, but this effect disappeared or reversed at longer delays.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept these condition-specific patterns. The editor notes the study 'demonstrates the boundaries of these proactive benefits' based on relatedness levels. Reviewer 1 states the results show 'when the changed item is very different from the original item there will be interference, and when the changed item is similar to the original item there will be facilitation.' Reviewer 2 describes how 'the direction of the effect can flip across the surface of relatedness values' and praises how 'the whole range of conditions is mapped to convincingly show' these patterns.

results.result: In the wider stimulus set at 48-hour delay, semantic relatedness between targets and cues showed a continuous relationship with memory outcomes: low relatedness produced proactive interference while high relatedness produced proactive facilitation. Intrusions decreased with increasing relatedness, supporting the remindings account.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies this as a weakness, noting 'in the finer scale results, the continuous relationship between the degree of relatedness and the degree of proactive facilitation/interference is less clear.' The relationship was 'only found in the wider stimulus set' and 'only when GloVe metric for measuring relatedness was used.' The absence of this relationship in the narrow stimulus set 'suggests this could be potentially an all-or-none effect (facilitation for related) rather than a matter of degree.' Reviewer 1 also notes the null result in the narrower set 'isn't clearly informative to the theory,' though acknowledges the positive result is 'consistent with the memory-for-change framework.'

results.result: In the ΔBoth condition where both cues and targets changed, there were no effects of combined cue+target relatedness on memorability in any experiment, though relatedness did improve interdependence in most experiments. Combined analyses across stimulus sets showed relatedness effects on interdependence but not consistently on memorability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these ΔBoth condition findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'performed teasing apart whether cue and target similarity separately influence memorability and interdependence seem to support the rest of their conclusions.' The pattern of interdependence effects being more consistent than memorability effects across conditions is acknowledged by Reviewer 2 as part of the overall findings.

results.result: Comparing retroactive and proactive designs, retroactive benefits were greater than proactive benefits in conditions showing facilitation, presumably because target responses receive retrieval practice during remindings. A flipped test experiment confirmed this advantage was not due to test order effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these between-experiment comparisons. Reviewer 1 notes the work is 'a companion piece to an earlier paper by Antony and colleagues (2022)' and that comparing the two 'is informative.' Reviewer 3 highlights 'the ability to directly compare the current results to their prior results on the retroactive effects of semantic relatedness' as a 'particular strength.' The interpretation about retrieval practice is accepted as the authors provide appropriate caveats about non-random assignment.

results.result: The results generally support predictions from Osgood's 1949 proposed surface regarding how relatedness affects memory interference and facilitation, though some predictions (such as no PI in the ΔCue condition) were not fully supported.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise the connection to Osgood's theory. Reviewer 1 states the work 'fills a gap in the prior literature regarding the cognitive validity of an 80-year-old proposal by Osgood' and notes 'the reader can see where the observed results match Osgood's theory and where they are inconclusive.' The editor describes this as advancing 'our understanding of how memories interact.' Reviewers accept that some aspects don't perfectly match Osgood's predictions but view this as informative rather than problematic.

results.result: The authors propose that pre-existing semantic relationships increase the likelihood of remindings during new learning, which results in retrieval practice benefits and opportunities to integrate memories. This mechanism explains the differential effects across conditions, with ΔCue showing more consistent facilitation than ΔTarget due to reduced competition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this theoretical interpretation. Reviewer 1 states 'the results are interpreted in terms of a set of existing theories, most prominently the memory-for-change framework, which proposes a mechanism (recursive reminding) potentially responsible for the facilitative effects.' Reviewer 3 notes the results are 'interpreted in the framework of recursive reminders (Hintzman, 2011)' and that 'interpretations and conclusions were mostly reasonable and included appropriate caveats.' The mechanistic explanation is viewed as consistent with the data patterns.

results.result: The study employed rigorous methodology with five experiments (N=1000 total), manipulating semantic relatedness (narrower vs. wider stimulus sets), delay (5 min vs. 48 hr), and type of change (ΔCue, ΔTarget, ΔBoth, No Δ, Control), with careful counterbalancing and large sample sizes.
results.evaluation: All reviewers praise the methodology. The editor highlights 'clean experimental design, rigorous statistics, large N samples, and well-characterized stimuli.' Reviewer 1 calls it 'a potential landmark' for manipulating 'multiple fundamental experimental characteristics using the same general experimental design.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'large N sample size, so both significant effects as well as null effects are robust and informative' and calls it 'a highly rigorous body of work that sets a great model for future studies.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the analyses were thorough and well-thought-out.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on learning acceleration findings (C3, C65-C72). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical methods and consistency across experiments. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this as an 'additional strength' showing relatedness leads to faster initial learning.

Strong agreement on methodology and experimental design (C7, C98-C110). Both evaluations find the design SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights well-controlled design with appropriate counterbalancing and sample sizes. Peer reviewers praise it as 'highly rigorous' with 'clean experimental design, rigorous statistics, large N samples' that 'sets a great model for future studies.'

Agreement on Osgood framework connections (C5-C6, C30-C33, C43, C93). Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the framework provides useful organization while identifying specific deviations. Peer reviewers praise this as 'filling a gap' regarding Osgood's 80-year-old proposal and view deviations as informative rather than problematic.

Agreement on ΔBoth condition findings (C61-C64). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the common metric addresses concerns about comparing different relatedness measures. Peer reviewers accept these findings as supporting the overall conclusions, noting interdependence effects are more consistent than memorability effects.

Divergent evaluations of retroactive-proactive comparisons (C73-C75, C85, C94). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to lack of random assignment and potential temporal confounds, though acknowledges authors provide appropriate caveats. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, praising the companion study design and accepting the comparisons with the caveats provided.

Agreement on condition-specific interference patterns (C44-C47). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical methods for PI under specific conditions (wider stimulus set, short delay, low relatedness). Peer reviewers accept these boundary conditions and praise how 'the whole range of conditions is mapped to convincingly show' the patterns.

Divergent evaluations of theoretical mechanisms (C8-C9, C86, C89, C91-C92). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting remindings were not directly measured and competing processes explanation is speculative. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the memory-for-change framework and recursive reminding interpretation as consistent with data patterns and appropriately caveated.

Agreement on interdependence findings (C52-C53, C58, C62, C64). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights consistent evidence that relatedness increases interdependence with appropriate correlation analyses. Peer reviewers emphasize this informs understanding of memory integration and note interdependence results are more converging than memorability results.

Divergent evaluations of continuous relatedness-memorability relationship (C48-C51). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, emphasizing significant correlations and tertile analyses showing crossover effect. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting the relationship was 'only found in the wider stimulus set' with GloVe metric, suggesting it 'could be potentially an all-or-none effect rather than a matter of degree.'

Agreement on flipped test control experiment (C76-C78). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this rules out testing order as explanation for retroactive-proactive differences. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the broader between-experiment comparisons that are viewed as informative.

Agreement on proactive facilitation as primary finding (C1-C2, C37-C43). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes converging statistical evidence from narrower stimulus set experiments. Peer reviewers describe this as 'compelling evidence' and a 'central result' showing facilitation is the rule with interference being the exception.

Agreement on ΔBoth condition null memorability findings (C59-C60). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes null results are properly reported with effect sizes and acknowledges dissociation from prior retroactive study. Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge as part of the teasing apart of cue and target similarity effects.

Partial overlap on intrusion findings (C54-C55). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the strong negative correlation between relatedness and intrusions contradicts simple interference accounts.
